Jane Bua
,
Madeleine Wulfahrt
,
Holden Seidlitz

You’re reading the Goings On newsletter, a guide to what we’re watching, listening to, and doing this week.
Sign up to receive it in your inbox.
Abraham Lincoln
never had much luck in theatres. But, this month, the number of big shows in the city which feature the sixteenth President will increase from one (“Oh, Mary!
,
” currently starring Bowen Yang, continues on Broadway) to two: an operatic adaptation of George Saunders’s
2017 novel
, also titled
“
Lincoln in the Bardo
,”
premières at the Metropolitan Opera on Oct. 19.
With music by Missy Mazzoli, “Lincoln in the Bardo” will be the first world première by a female composer at the Met since it was founded, in 1883. The story takes place during the course of one evening, in a hazy spiritual plane where anguished souls are caught between life and the hereafter. Lincoln’s son Willie, who died of typhoid fever at just eleven years old, is one of those stuck in stasis. The set depicts the wooded Oak Hill Cemetery, where Willie was temporarily interred after his death—and to which Mazzoli has an honorary key—but the stage is fragmented into a layered arrangement, segments contoured with neon lighting. “People are moving between a real landscape and void space,” the director, Lileana Blain-Cruz, said. “We wanted to keep the lines blurry.”
Illustration by Diego Mallo
As Willie wanders the cemetery, he encounters others similarly unable to move forward. “There are a hundred and sixty-six attributions in the novel,” the librettist, Royce Vavrek, said. “The other ghosts, I wish I could have included all of them.” But a number of them still appear in the background, wearing costumes that reflect how they died—carriage tracks across the torso, garments singed from a fire. Some souls are trapped by the Bardo’s “tendrils,” which are brought to life with a little help from James Ortiz, the puppet designer who created Rocky, the alien, for “Project Hail Mary.” Those who have been fully overtaken by the Bardo, with no hope of escape, are entrapped in giant puppet suits.
The adaptation, despite its sober subject, includes some dazzling pyrotechnics—specifically, at the moment when Willie’s soul crosses into the beyond. This transfiguration, which Saunders called the matterlightblooming phenomenon, is described in the book as a “blinding flash of light” with a “firesound.” “We went through moments of, like, Is it a smoke thing? No, that’s boring,” Blain-Cruz said. “Is it a projection thing? No, we can see that. Is it a confetti thing? No, because then you’re leaving the remains behind. A spirit leaves nothing.” The resulting spectacle includes a thirty-foot firework. “We’ve gone through many safety talks,” she said.
There are few things more American than fireworks; the opera is, after all, part of the Met’s celebration of the country’s two-hundred-and-fiftieth birthday (with select performances through Nov. 14). Set amid the devastations of slavery and war, though, “Lincoln in the Bardo” is not exactly patriotic. But, Blain-Cruz said, “My hope is that, in this portrait of a particularly fraught American moment, with particularly fraught human beings, we can be reminded that everyone deserves love and dignity.”—
Jane Bua
About Town
Movies
Until the dawn of the talkies, a movie without live music was rare. The streets of “Metropolis” thrummed with orchestral flourishes; countless pianists found their own special sounds for Charlie Chaplin’s walk. Now it’s once again fashionable to screen silent films with live accompaniment.
“
Instruments of Desire
,”
a new film series with chamber music, at the Roxy Cinema (through at least November), asks, What if music were the amuse-bouche to a movie? The curators, Kamron Saniee and Emilie Meyer, pair films about music with musicians: “The Draughtsman’s Contract,” from 1982, by Peter Greenaway, is preceded with a performance by the New York Recorder Guild (Nov. 5); Todd Field’s 2022 thriller, “Tár,” will have a performance by the Candide Quartet (Nov. 19).—
Madeleine Wulfahrt
Experimental Pop
Last year, the Baltimore experimental-pop band
Animal Collective
celebrated the twentieth anniversary of its psychedelic masterpiece “Feels,” from 2005. The four multi-instrumentalists, all of whom use aliases—Avey Tare, Panda Bear, Geologist, and Deakin—had not performed together in a few years. Now they’re playing a proper reunion for four nights only, in New York, Los Angeles, and Pomona. With a special guest each night, the freak-folk opera of strange tunings, blooming drones, sputtery percussion, and ecstatic hooks will feature favorites like “Flesh Canoe,” “Bees,” and the eight-and-a-half-minute “Banshee Beat.” It’s almost impossible to fathom the sounds’ live reconstitution, so catch the spectacle while you can.—
Holden Seidlitz (
Knockdown Center
; Oct. 21-22.)
Alt Rock
Ecca Vandal.Photograph by Sean McDonald
The South African-born, Melbourne-raised musician
Ecca Vandal
sprang up in the mid-twenty-tens welding together punk rock and hip-hop, using her voice as a soldering iron. Her style was multifaceted and gloriously chaotic, but bystanders to the havoc wreaked by the sound wanted her to narrow her focus in a specific direction. Amid all the noise surrounding her process, she unplugged for several years to reconnect with her inner voice. Her 2026 album, “Looking for People to Unfollow,” which arrived nearly a decade after her self-titled début, is an epic reaffirmation of purpose. More distinctive and dynamic, the LP is searing even in its quieter moments, documenting an artist relentlessly moving forward.—
Sheldon Pearce (
Bowery Ballroom
; Oct. 17.)
Art
The new show by
Malcolm Peacock
is a site at which to practice a certain reverence: laid flat on the gallery floor are two portraits asking us to kneel, to grow humble enough to be with them. Two Black men are rendered in graphite, eyes closed, mouths open with yearning, disclosing sighs of ecstasy or prayer. Nearby is a semicircular sculpture, a reliquary-like architecture containing two more portraits—four more closed, withholding eyes. The exterior of the sculpture is adorned with synthetic braids, a fundamental material with Peacock, for whom braiding is a metaphor for relation, an embrace, irreducible intimacy. Braids are referred to as a protective style, and indeed the portraits inside the sculpture partake in a sense of safety: the structure is somewhere between a cradle and a chapel—one anointed with the unction of Black adornment.—
Zoë Hopkins (
Sikkema Malloy Jenkins
; through Oct. 24.)
Dance
Surupa Sen and Daquil Miriyala in “Khankhana.”Photograph by Naveen V. Raju
It’s a bountiful week for Indian classical dance. For decades, the
Nrityagram Dance Ensemble
—hailing from its own dance village, outside of Bengaluru—has been New York’s favorite provider of Odissi, a form of sinuous shapes and vivid storytelling. The troupe’s last visit to the Joyce Theatre, in 2023, lacked the dancing of its brilliant choreographer, Surupa Sen, but
this time
(Oct. 13-18) she’s dancing again. Over at Danspace Project (Oct. 15), the Kerala-born
Sreelakshmy Govardhanan
presents a solo concert in the South Indian form Kuchipudi. What’s Kuchipudi? Govardhanan explains via interspersed commentary, and in a post-show conversation with the
New Yorker
contributor Marina Harss.—
Brian Seibert
Movies
A crucial oral history merges with a joyful party in
“Once Upon a Time in Harlem,”
a project of epochal scope, from 1972, which is nonetheless a new movie. That year, the Harlem-born filmmaker William Greaves gathered, in a town house belonging to Duke Ellington, a wide array of luminaries who’d been part of the Harlem Renaissance half a century earlier, including Eubie Blake, James Van Der Zee, Regina Andrews, and Arna Bontemps. Greaves assembled a team of cinematographers (including his son, David) to film the reunion, and the resulting torrent of reminiscences, tussle between varying perspectives, and wealth of spontaneous musical interludes revitalize the era’s artistic and political passions with a startling, thrilling immediacy. The film was left incomplete when William Greaves died, in 2014; David directed the completion, which is among the greatest of documentaries.—
Richard Brody (Opening Oct. 16 at
Film Forum
.)
Bar Tab
Taran Dugal cheers on the New York Liberty in Williamsburg.
Illustration by Patricia Bolaños
New York hoops fans, rejoice: your year of playoffs hysteria isn’t over yet. Sure, it was a Knicks summer, but orange leaves are falling now, and with autumn comes a new home-town underdog to rally for: the W.N.B.A.’s New York Liberty. On a recent Sunday, two friends inaugurated the team’s postseason playoffs run at
Blazers
, a bar in Williamsburg dedicated to women’s sports. They made their way to the back room, where the floor had been painted with orange court markings, and settled at a table in two-point territory. The décor surpassed that of a typical sports bar, dingy novelty signs replaced by a mural of Katie Ledecky, Simone Biles, Serena Williams, and Allyson Felix. Above a gargantuan television hung on the rear wall, a disco ball levitated inside a regulation-size hoop. Boos sounded as the opposition, the Minnesota Lynx, took the court. At tipoff, the guests’ beers arrived: frosty Guinness, refreshing Talea Al Dente; Lynx’s ball. The duo finger-licked their way through a bucket of Buffalo wings as the Liberty had an early hot streak; they devoured a burger during the second quarter, its gooey pepper jack a small consolation amid a brutal Minnesota run. At halftime, they wandered into the Trailblazer Room, a closetlike space painted with dozens of portraits of female athletes, and snapped a selfie in the mirror as Gabby Douglas smiled behind them. Perhaps it was the clipped pace of the game, or maybe the Ellie’s Purse Handler—a scrumptious cocktail of gin, elderflower, lemon, and cava—that made the second half fly by. As the clock wound down on a Liberty blowout, “Let’s Groove,” by Earth, Wind & Fire, started up. “That’s the secret,” one man said to his girlfriend, who was dancing a celebratory twist by the foul line. “It’s all in the knees!”

By
Helen Rosner
You’re reading the Food Scene newsletter, Helen Rosner’s guide to what, where, and how to eat.
Sign up to receive it in your inbox.
Gertrude Aronow, the grandmother of the restaurateur Nate Adler, was, by Adler’s account, an eccentric woman of uncommon charisma, the sort of person who made any room feel like a party. Adler and his wife-cum-business partner, Rachel Jackson, who together own the group
RAD
Restaurants, have graced three establishments with variations on Aronow’s name, all of them devoted to a sort of modern version of Ashkenazi American cooking. Gertie began as a Jewish diner in Williamsburg and was recently reborn in Prospect Heights, as a bagel shop. Gertrude’s, down the street, is a playful bistro with duck pastrami and challah-bread Parker House rolls. And now there is Trudie’s Tavern, which opened this past summer in Carroll Gardens, a smart little restaurant that’s the most ambitious, and the most accomplished, of the three.
For sixteen years, before it was Trudie’s, this sunny Court Street corner was Buttermilk Channel, a restaurant famous as much for its status as a pioneer of the Brooklyn restaurant culture of the late two-thousands as it was for its magnificent fried chicken. When it closed, in 2024, the owner, Doug Crowell, joked that if he were doing it all again, he’d skip the white tablecloths, and it’s true that the ritziness that they connoted was a bit out of synch with the comfort-food menu. But I always liked them, and the softening effect of their snowy drape on what was often a clattery, raucous room. I was delighted to see white tablecloths at Trudie’s, too, though the open rectangle of space has also been tamed by a few strategically placed half-height walls, which lend a sense of intimacy. The décor is pleasingly colorful: pink napkins on the tables, blue velvet upholstering the chairs and banquettes, a pink sky filling an enormous painting of swans against the gentle brown of a wood-panelled wall.
If you wanted Trudie’s to be romantic, as the pink and the linens might imply it to be, there’s a romantic restaurant in there for you: a dirty Martini, a plate of oysters, a lusty strip steak dripping in bone-marrow butter. But it’s also a casual restaurant, good for a burger and a beer with a friend, or an early dinner with the kids—my three-year-old and I both, one evening, were transfixed by the old tube TV mounted over the bar, which streams classic movies with wobbly warmth. It’s a little kitschy, too: the bathroom, with eighties-era baseball memorabilia and multicolored party lighting, gave me haunting flashbacks to the many bar mitzvahs I attended in my youth. Families stream in for the early seatings; dates and double dates take over the tables as the evening sets in. I’m not entirely sure what sort of restaurant Trudie’s thinks it is, or wants to be, or how exactly it wants me to feel, but—oddly—that ambiguity works out into its own quite wonderful thing: a bit of poise, a bit of roughness, a not quite emulsified admixture of crisply ironed and easygoing.
The menu is a similar mishmash. You’ve got comfort-food elements that speak to the “Tavern” part of the restaurant’s name, such as a huge puffy pretzel dotted with salt or hunky pigs in a blanket rolled in everything-bagel seasoning. But there’s something more sophisticated happening in the kitchen, evident in such dishes as a swordfish on a late-summer pool of pepper-and-watermelon gazpacho, and a potato pancake extravagantly dressed in a dill-and-cucumber crème fraîche and strewn with smoked trout and orange bubbles of flying-fish roe. It’s a latke, of course, even if the menu doesn’t call it one. Trudie’s is the least overtly Jewish of the couple’s three restaurants, but the menu is woven with the motifs of American Jewish cuisine: egg noodles, cucumber salad, schmaltz for miles, droplets of it even floating on top of a Martini. One of the things that I like best about these spots is how they play on memory and tradition without getting hokey or shticky or—the worst possible restaurant sin—maudlin. Trudie’s offers snow crab, three marshmallow-white claws served chilled on ice, with a bit of dijonnaise for dipping. It’s a preparation lifted directly from the Miami Beach fixture Joe’s Stone Crab, which, though utterly unkosher in virtually every way, is arguably the most Jewish restaurant in the city’s history, at least in a Philip Roth kind of way.
A sherry cobbler.
Helen, Help Me!
E-mail your questions
about dining, eating, and anything food-related, and Helen may respond in a future newsletter.
The menu, overseen by the chef Mike Cain, is largely playing the hits. One night I paused, knife in position over a steak, to watch a platter of roast chicken travel through the dining room, burnished and glossy alongside a crisp pile of roasted potatoes. It was served with a white-and-green scoop of creamy cucumber salad flecked with dill (a recipe from Adler’s other grandmother) and an entire gravy boat of what I would discover, ordering the dish on my next visit, was a dense, onion-sweet chicken gravy, with just a hint of sharp, vinegary kick. Best of all was the lamb schnitzel, perhaps the restaurant’s biggest swing. Schnitzel is usually the province of subtler, tenderer meats—your chicken breasts, your veal rounds. But, pounded thin, breaded, and fried, served under lashings of sweet-sharp blackberry sauce, with a confetti of whole blackberries and leaves of mint, the lamb version was brilliant and bizarre, a symphony of strong-willed flavors. It put me in mind of a meal that might be found in a lush and gently ominous Mitteleuropa folk tale, and also, a little bit, of a cowboy-style chicken-fried steak.
The portions are hearty, but it would be a mistake to skip the side dishes, a broad selection of salads, cooked vegetables, and other odds and ends that showcase some of the kitchen’s surest work. You could make a meal of an utterly dreamy bowl of garlicky braised Rancho Gordo butter beans, paired with the Schmaltz Fried Rice, gleaming and toothsome and studded with bits of crispy gribenes, and maybe a fresh green salad—dressed simply in a bright, sunny vinaigrette—to cut through all the richness. Wedges of rotisserie-cooked cabbage, in a funky, anchovy-rich vinaigrette, could maybe stand a bit more fire. (So, on some nights, could the service, which drifts a bit to the spacey side of welcoming.) Save room, as well, for a banana split with pretzel-infused ice cream, or a slice of cake, three towering layers of carrot sponge, with a coconut filling and a dense cream-cheese frosting. It’s the whole restaurant in one slice: sweet and not-too-sweet, happily a bit of one thing and happily a bit of another. ♦

Comment
Donald Trump After the Midterms
If the coming election does result in a blue wave, Trump will be faced with the fact of his diminishment. The rest of us will be faced with the wreckage.
By
David Remnick
Photo illustration by Cristiana Couceiro; Source photographs from Getty
Signs of a midterm blue wave are everywhere, and yet it would be journalistic malpractice not to attach some nervous caveats to any prediction. Polls are sketchy. Campaigns have never been more subject to the desires of the wealthy. What is more, the President of the United States has the impulse control of a toddler, though most toddlers have neither the authority nor the inclination to spark an insurrection, destabilize the Western alliance, live-stream an execution, or threaten to end “a whole civilization.” We are subjected daily to the caprices of a mind both unregulated and amoral. As Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has said, the Commander-in-Chief is “fascist to the core.” You may prefer milder terminology. Fine. But, after a decade defined by Donald Trump’s unceasing presence, a growing percentage of the American electorate appears to recognize the uniqueness of this President and the mayhem that he has instigated from the Oval Office.
We are, collectively, on guard against undue optimism. Still, if the coming election does result in a blue wave, Trump will be faced with the fact of his diminishment. The rest of us will be faced with the wreckage.
A decade ago, those who believed that Trump’s ascent represented a grave and multifaceted danger, a national emergency, were often met with sneering dismissal. The right generally regarded Trump’s most vocal opponents as pussy-hatted snowflakes, woke snobs indifferent to the struggles of working people. They were, in a word, “deranged.” Some on the left, too, insisted that those who thought of Trump as aberrant and sought nightly salvation in a tankard of Chardonnay and “The Rachel Maddow Show” ignored America’s complicated legacy. Was Trump really so much worse than his predecessors? Hardly! In fact, he was practically mainstream, “not some strange eddy in the current of American history,” one knowing essayist wrote in
The New Republic
. “He is where the ordinary river flowed.” All that distinguished Trump was “aesthetics”—“He is vulgar. He is rude.”
In the passage from lame duck to pensioner, Trump still has plenty of time to inflict further damage on the Republic while milking it for profit. He is the sum of his whims and his rages, and, a change in Congress or not, he will likely go on flouting the law, tightening the screws on universities, cultural institutions, and the press. What he seems to value most of late is the humiliation of his enemies and, even more, the accumulation of vast wealth. Since the second Inauguration, the Trumps and their satraps have operated with all the commercial cunning of the Corleone family; the White House is their front, their Genco Pura Olive Oil Company. The Attorney General, Todd Blanche, is an obedient Tom Hagen. Recently, Kristen Welker, of NBC’s “Meet the Press,” asked Blanche, “If the President asks you to do something that you feel crosses an ethical or legal line, would you do it?” Blanche replied, “The President will never ask me to do something unethical or illegal. He never has. He never will.” Not a wartime consigliere, perhaps, but Blanche understands the expectations of his Don.
Every week brings word of a new grift, a new meme coin, a Melania doc, a pay-for-access club, or fresh funds from Gulf grandees looking for leverage. The other day, we learned that Kimberly Guilfoyle, Donald, Jr.,’s ex and the U.S. Ambassador to Greece, texted a
maga
donor insisting that he pay off her hundred-thousand-dollar Amex bill in exchange for favors from, in no particular order, the I.R.S., Tucker Carlson, and Kid Rock. (Guilfoyle has disputed the authenticity of the messages, which include, “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.”) But who cares? The Administration counts on an exhausted nation’s distraction. This may well have been the singular lesson that Trump absorbed from his moral instructor, Roy Cohn: if you keep up a steady stream of bullshit, if you keep denying and counterattacking, all of Monday’s trespasses will be forgotten by Tuesday.
There are signs that the President is unravelling, in ways that are different from late-period Joe Biden but are alarming all the same. It’s not so much the thickening ankles as it is the loosening inhibitions. Nearly every morning, the
Daily Beast
publishes headlines that archly reflect the situation: “Confused Trump, 80, Makes Bizarre Blunder in Late-Night Meltdown”; “Sleepless Trump, 80, Goes Full Disney Adult in 1 A.M. Posting Frenzy”; “Trump, 80, Repeatedly Slumps in Chair Ahead of Midterm Blitz.”
What more and more voters are coming to understand is how profoundly they have been betrayed. And this is not just about the price of gas and groceries, though “affordability” is scarcely the joke the President thinks it is. Vladimir Putin long ago set out to mock the United States for its hypocrisies.
You are no better than us
—that was his message and his cover to crush dissent at home and the liberties of an independent Ukraine. When Trump threatens Greenland and Canada or greases a media merger in his interest, he is proving Putin’s point. When the titans of tech obediently line up at Trump’s Inauguration and fund his ballroom, Putin smiles. Who are we to lecture him about oligarchy? This is the ethos of the era defined by Putin and Trump: morality in politics is for dupes; all that matters is interests. Because Trump is simultaneously an autocrat and a performance artist, because Americans tend to cling reflexively to the fraying notion of national exceptionalism, it is difficult to reckon with the idea that a President might be not merely shambolic and incompetent but something far darker, even evil.
But if we are uncomfortable using a word like “evil,” how else are we to describe the spectacle of the President unleashing Elon Musk, the wealthiest person in the history of humankind, to slash the budget of the U.S. Agency for International Development? According to an article in
The Lancet
and the intensive research of Atul Gawande, a surgeon, a former assistant administrator for U.S.A.I.D., and a writer for this magazine, the agency’s support—focussed on fighting malaria, polio, malnutrition, tuberculosis, and H.I.V.—saved at least ninety million lives in the previous two decades. Researchers estimate that the cruelty-by-budget-cut has been responsible for the loss of as many as seven hundred thousand lives.
This is among the many depredations that this supposedly mainstream Administration has committed. In 1788, at a ratifying convention in Richmond, James Madison defended the newly drafted Constitution, but warned that its fulfillment would depend on the quality of the people as well as the document’s written principles. “To suppose that any form of Government will secure liberty or happiness without any virtue in the people,” he said, “is a chimerical idea.” Election Day is November 3rd. In some states, voting has already begun. ♦

The Boards
Kramer and Fauci—Enemies to Friends to Protagonists
The playwright and the immunologist famously argued about AIDs live on C-SPAN, in 1993. Their heated exchange now unfolds in a new play that almost included a “Guys and Dolls” song break.
By
Michael Schulman
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
The bond between Anthony Fauci and Larry Kramer is one of history’s happy riddles. Fauci (immunologist, public-health official, mensch) and Kramer (writer,
AIDS
activist, crank) began as adversaries. In 1988, Kramer, angry about the government’s sluggish H.I.V. research, wrote an open letter that called Fauci, then the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, an “incompetent idiot.” But they became wary allies. “I quickly realized that despite his sometimes provocative behavior, he was as noble as the most respected scientist and public servant,” Fauci wrote later. During the first Bush Administration, Kramer urged Fauci to chain himself to the White House fence. (He declined.) In 2020, Fauci, newly famous as the
COVID
pandemic’s explainer-in-chief, called Kramer, who was dying. “I love you, Tony,” Kramer said, weakly. “I love you, Larry,” Fauci replied.
Between these endpoints of hate and love came an hour-long C-
SPAN
broadcast, on November 30, 1993, in which the men quarrelled, teased, and fielded calls. The Clinton Administration had just announced an
AIDS
task force, which Fauci hoped would hasten drug development; Kramer, piped in on a janky remote line, slammed Fauci’s “bureaucratic bullshit” and called Clinton a “big wuss.” “I probably have a more complicated relationship with Tony than anybody in my entire life,” Kramer said. “He is a man, an ordinary man, who was being asked to play God, and he is being punished because he cannot be God.”
Not long after Kramer died, the theatre director Daniel Fish came across the video and was riveted. “There’s something about two people who are able to really argue and still pay attention and listen to each other that tragically no longer exists,” Fish said recently. He was at St. Ann’s Warehouse, in Dumbo, where “Kramer/Fauci,” his piece drawn from the transcript, is playing. He was joined, after a tech rehearsal, by the actors Thomas Jay Ryan (Kramer) and Will Brill (Fauci), who wear earpieces onstage that play the 1993 audio, “like we’re singing along to an hour-long song,” Brill said.
Fish, known for his darkly sexy take on “Oklahoma!,” didn’t alter the text but toys with it like Silly Putty. The actress Jennifer Seastone, who plays all the callers, appears on Rollerblades, or in a chicken costume. Halfway through, Brill pulls out a machine that fills the stage with foam, submerging the actors in a cumulus of bubbles. (“It’s something that I’ve been interested in using onstage for a long time,” Fish explained.) Other theatrical flourishes died in rehearsal. They’d discussed Kramer and Fauci pausing to sing “Sue Me,” from “Guys and Dolls.” (“You promise me this, / You promise me that!”) “There was a moment when we had a kiss,” Brill recalled. “We never actually did nudity, but we did talk about nudity.”
Neither actor went for an exact impersonation, although Brill approximates Fauci’s Brooklyn accent. Brill spent the first stretch of the pandemic in Hell’s Kitchen, getting over both
COVID
and a breakup, occasionally turning on Fauci’s briefings. “I admired his knowledge and his ability to be stoic and politic, even when surrounded by absolute buffoonery,” he said. Ryan’s connection to Kramer was personal. He moved to New York in the mid-eighties, as a young gay actor, and read Kramer’s anti-Reagan screeds. “I was scared of all of it,” Ryan said. “I couldn’t hear any of it, because he was too scary a figure.”
They pulled up a clip of the 1993 broadcast:
K
RAMER
: Tony, if you say, “More has been learned about this virus than any virus in the history of mankind,” I’m gonna come down there.
F
AUCI
: I know, Larry, that’s why I’m not gonna say it. I’m afraid you’re gonna come down here!
“The way that Larry makes Tony laugh is so cute,” Brill said.
“But every time a moment of warmth like that happens, Larry will jerk the rug,” Ryan observed.
They watched a second clip: July 29, 2026, when an older, wearier Fauci was summoned to the Senate. Josh Hawley, attempting to shame the doctor, asks him such questions as “What color tie are you wearing?” as Fauci repeatedly takes the Fifth. “It’s so tough to watch,” Brill said, choking up, “because we’ve seen Tony speak so eloquently with someone who is truly intellectually sparring with him, and this shit was so disingenuous.”
When “Kramer/Fauci” was staged in February, at the N.Y.U. Skirball Center, Fauci went to the opening night, along with Kramer’s widower,
ACT UP
veterans, and some burly security men. “Tony said that we all did a good job,” Brill recalled. He described Fauci telling the actors about another contentious appearance with Kramer. “Larry was really lighting into him very badly on TV, and Tony was very shaken by it,” Brill said. “He got home, and the moment he walked in the door, he picked up the phone, and Larry said, ‘Weren’t we so good today?’ ” ♦

Paris Postcard
The First Candid
In 1838, Louis Daguerre snapped a photo of a Parisian street, empty but for a shoeshine boy and his client. Now that some sleuths have zeroed in on the location, the city is marking it with a plaque.
By
Lauren Collins
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
Before August Sander and Diane Arbus and Olan Mills, before Facetune and duck face, there were two: a shoeshine boy and his client, captured by Louis Daguerre on the Boulevard du Temple in 1838, in what is thought to be the first photograph to depict human beings. The bootblack squats beside a chest containing the tools of his trade. The patron stands, hands clasped behind his back, with a foot perched on the box. We know it’s spring, because the leaves are coming in on the plane trees. The two were hardly the only people out that day on the bustling stretch of cabarets. But they were the only people who held still long enough to be captured by Daguerre’s curious new machine, which required an exposure time of up to ten minutes. The next year, presenting the daguerreotype to the Assemblée Nationale, the physicist François Arago noted, “In this genre, it’s the unforeseen that one must count upon.” Soon, the French state would buy the rights to the invention and offer it as a free gift “to the world.” The names of the boy and his client were never recorded, but they live on as the accidental embodiment of photography on the brink of conquering the world.
One night in 2024, Maximilien Van Aertryck went out for drinks with his colleagues Axel Danielson and Kalle Boman. Van Aertryck is a producer who works with the Swedish filmmaker Ruben Östlund and has co-directed a documentary about the history of image-making. In other words, he knows a lot about photography. He had always loved the Daguerre picture: “It’s so poetic, with those two lonely people on that huge frame.” As he and his friends drifted out of the café, they crossed the Boulevard du Temple. It was June. The trees were nearing lushness. “We were, like, ‘Wait a minute! It must have been taken somewhere around here!,’ ” Van Aertryck recalled, visiting the area the other day. They punched a few keywords into Google, and found some articles, “in pretty big newspapers,” surmising that the photograph might have been snapped near the Filles du Calvaire Métro stop. “We knew immediately that there was no way it was there,” Van Aertryck said. “If you look at the photo, it just doesn’t make sense. So we went home and went to bed, promising that we’d meet at the same place at eight the next morning, and we’d figure this out.”
“Just like a Cro-Mag to bring a club to a rock fight.”
Cartoon by P. C. Vey
Thus began an eighteen-month quest to pinpoint the exact location of the shot, involving everything from archival research to drones to very long measuring tapes. It wasn’t easy. For one thing, Baron Haussmann had demolished swaths of the neighborhood in the mid-eighteen-hundreds to create the Place de la République. Van Aertryck and his colleagues turned to prints, paintings, real-estate registers, and topographical maps to re-create Daguerre’s environs, but these pre-photographic renderings had their limits. “We kept just finding engravings of one particular building, because some emperor got shot there,” Van Aertryck recalled. Both Daguerre’s workshop, on what is now Rue Léon-Jouhaux, and a theatre that he owned, called the Diorama, burned in 1839. “No one, not even the biggest nerds who have researched this,” can agree on where, exactly, Daguerre took the photograph, Van Aertryck said, but he and his team were able to determine that three buildings from the era are still standing today. They brought their findings to an architectural firm, which used a 3-D scan of the entire square to triangulate the shoeshiner’s location. Another architectural firm, using the same data, homed in on a point just a few feet away. “We decided to split the difference,” Van Aertryck explained, scuffing his shoe over a red “X” that had been painted on one of the paving stones, not far from some wads of gum. “A colleague ran out to buy nail polish to mark the spot!” he explained.
For nearly a century, the Bavarian National Museum, in Munich, possessed a photographic plate of the image, which Daguerre had sent to King Ludwig I, but it was badly damaged by restoration efforts during the Second World War—the only remaining physical trace of “Boulevard du Temple” is a photo of the photo that the
MoMA
curator Beaumont Newhall took in the nineteen-thirties. On October 15th, however, the City of Paris will unveil a plaque commemorating the shoeshine pair—an “unforeseen” detail, the world’s first photographic portrait sitters and the original photobombers at the same time. “I hope people will make it theirs and embrace it as the starting point for something,” Van Aertryck said. May it spawn a million selfies. ♦

At the Rink
Kash Patel’s Slap Shot
The F.B.I. director’s hockey team, the Dons, faced their rivals in a beer league. With rogue slap shots and hovering security agents, Patel was in the zone—or, at least, next to it.
By
Richie McGinniss
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
The F.B.I. director, Kash Patel, faced an icy Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing last month, in which both parties pressed him on a string of blunders—taxpayer-funded travel, mishandling of the Epstein files, loosened hiring rules involving bestiality, the boozy photo op he’d had with the gold-winning United States men’s Olympic hockey team in Milan. As Senator Mazie Hirono phrased it, “You have wasted untold taxpayer dollars driving around in foreign luxury cars, partying in Italy, and flying a private jet to play golf and watch hockey.”
Incomplete statement—he also spends a lot of time
playing
hockey. Earlier this year, in a locker room in Virginia, Patel, who is forty-six, laced his skates before a beer-league championship game at the MedStar Capitals Iceplex, in Arlington. He slipped on his red-white-and-blue jersey for his team, the Dons; a patch on it reads “Don’t Tread on Me”; another bears the logo “
K
$
H.
”
Patel, though young for an F.B.I. director, is old for the league. Regarded by his fellow-players as somewhat clumsy on the ice, he makes up for his lack of speed with a decent slap shot and a willingness to throw himself down, spread-eagled, to block pucks. He tore a biceps this way in a championship three years ago. (He joked that he’d hurt it “kicking the shit out of the deep state.”)
The Dons went unbeaten over multiple seasons in a lesser division, but they hadn’t won the crown since moving up to the top division, two years before. The opposition: a team called the Hat Trick Swayzes, whose jerseys bear the image of “Point Break”-era Patrick Swayze. One of the Swayzes’ defensemen is the thirty-eight-year-old Karl Alzner, a first-round N.H.L. draft pick in 2007, who spent most of his career with the Washington Capitals. Alzner reminisced about watching his dad’s beer-league games as a kid, “coming to the rink early in the morning and seeing a garbage can full of beer cans.”
After suiting up, a conservative member of the Swayzes, who used to wear faux jean-short shells, offered a rousing pre-game speech. “There are tens of millions of people across the country who, if they knew this game was happening tonight, would be rooting for the Swayzes to beat Kash Patel and the Dons. Tonight, we are all libs!” His teammates roared.
Patel had surpassed Alzner as the most famous person at the rink. A relative unknown when he joined the Dons, in 2014, he’s now a household name, the butt of jokes on late-night television. These days, a pack of F.B.I. agents with earpieces are posted by the locker room, and armored BMWs sit outside. The opposition tends to be respectful, although once, when Patel chased a puck into a corner, an opponent yelled out, “Epstein didn’t kill himself!” (“You know a suicide when you see one,” Patel has said.)
Typically, the F.B.I. agents guarding the director outnumber the spectators at ten-thirty on a Sunday night, but this time there were about twenty civilians in the stands. Within a minute of the puck hitting the ice, the Dons surrendered the first breakaway. Patel was no help. In the third period, with his team trailing, his ice time was limited, but, during one of his few shifts, a pass came from behind the net and went through his legs for a Swayzes goal. The Swayzes were victorious.
Just after Patel’s Senate grilling, the Dons faced off against the Swayzes in the championship again. Things kicked off hot in the first period. Patel whiffed a shot attempt at the blue line, swinging his stick wildly. Somehow, he had enough time to recalibrate and fire off one of his unruly slap shots, hurling it way off target. Dom Gurshman, a former pro for a Finnish team who now plays defense for the Swayzes, recalled, “After Kash’s whiffed shot, I thought we’d get a signature rim down the wall. I was standing seven feet wide of the net, almost facing the corner, and the shot clipped my shin pads and went in. I was shocked.” Patel had scored.
The Dons took the lead, and by the end of the night their victory was assured. But, with seconds left on the clock, Patel wanted to get in one last slap shot. He gathered the puck behind his own net. His teammates hooted from the bench. He fired it off and it ricocheted around the boards. The horns sounded; the Dons had won.
During the handshake, the director wore a wide, toothy grin that had not been seen in public since he partied with the Olympians in Italy. Though a shakeup in the midterms might well mess with the routines of loyal Trump appointees like Patel, on this night, chugging beers on the rooftop at the rink, Kash was king. The F.B.I. agents waited patiently. ♦
An earlier version of this article inaccurately described the inspiration of the Dons’ name.

Globe-Trotting Dept.
Around the World in Explorer Names
The American Geographical Society has long invited big-name adventurers—Amelia Earhart, Neil Armstrong—to sign its ceremonial globe. The latest? Astronaut Kathryn Sullivan.
By
Sarah Larson
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
At the Explorers Club, uptown, the American Geographical Society, founded in 1851, celebrated its hundred-and-seventy-fifth year one recent evening by observing its most sacred ritual: a ceremonial globe signing. The society’s Fliers & Explorers Globe, donated in 1929 by the
Times
editor and A.G.S. president John Finley, was signed by many of his era’s most renowned explorers, including Charles Lindbergh, Amelia Earhart, and Sir Edmund Hillary. “Finley interviewed people who came in from their expeditions, and he’d get them to sign it,” Jerome Dobson, an A.G.S. president emeritus, said. His necktie had an antique-map print. Later, the globe was signed by John Glenn, Neil Armstrong, the Apollo 8 crew, and others. That night, it would be signed by the oceanographer, former Navy captain, and retired astronaut Kathryn Sullivan—the first person to both walk in outer space and visit the deepest point of the ocean, in the Mariana Trench.
During cocktail hour, a spiffily dressed group of eminent geographers gathered in the library bar around a Fliers & Explorers replica—a party globe, perhaps. “This is the globe you can touch,” Marie Price, the current A.G.S. president, said. “Spin it around!” (“Let’s not go wild,” Dobson said.) The library had an icy-exploration theme: taxidermied polar bear, signed Shackleton portrait, Admiral Peary’s ice pick, snowy painting of bedraggled men by a tent. “That looks like one of our camp trips, huh, Lee?” Price said to Lee Schwartz, a former
GOTUS
(Geographer of the United States).
When Dobson joined A.G.S., in 1997, the Fliers & Explorers Globe was underappreciated, he said. “I didn’t even notice it,” he recalled. “It was on a spindly shaft in the corner; we’d go spin it.” It hadn’t seen much action since Glenn had signed it, at the White House, in front of J.F.K., Lyndon Johnson, “and two of Bobby Kennedy’s children—not the one currently in government.” Seeing an opportunity, Dobson had proposed new signings. “Who wouldn’t consider it an honor?” he said. “So we invited Neil Armstrong; Don Walsh and Jacques Piccard, the first people to go to the bottom of the Mariana Trench; and Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones, who first circumnavigated the globe in a balloon.” (Were the Piccards inspiration for Captain Picard, of “Star Trek”? “I never thought of that,” Price said.) The retired Coast Guard captain Lawson Brigham, who resembled a seafaring Lee Iacocca, approached the globe. “I signed through the Bering Strait, but I had been at the North Pole and the South Pole,” he said, pointing. “As close to the South Pole as you get on a Coast Guard icebreaker.”
“Lawson did the circumnavigation pole to pole, not the most common way to go,” Price said. “You need an icebreaker.” (“There is a precedent—names on here of pilots who went that way,” Dobson said.) Nearby, wearing a waterproof modern-adventurer hat, the eighty-five-year-old G.P.S. pioneer Charlie Trimble chatted about trying to determine whether Mt. Everest was rising or sinking. (Rising, he said.)
During the main event, in a ballroom, Sullivan, a capable-looking seventy-five-year-old with a blond bob and a dark jacket and slacks, approached the globe, accepted a Sharpie, and said, “Right under my very good friend and shipmate Don Walsh.” People craned their necks. A partygoer whispered, “Where do you sign the globe if you’re an astronaut?”
Afterward, Sullivan retired to the terrace. Deep-sea exploration, she said, “is not a bad analogue for going into space.” Both require a vehicle “that can take your squishy little body to a place that it clearly doesn’t belong. I’m comfortable inside, and I look through a window and know that right out there I would die. How is it possible for me to be here, eating my tuna-fish sandwich?” She went to Challenger Deep, the bottom of the trench, in 2020. “The word that kept coming to mind was ‘moonscape,’ ” she said. “A fine, silty sediment, gently rolling bottom, a little more tan than the gray of the moon”; barren, to our eyes, with “typically unsexy critters like burrowing worms.” As for space, “It’s a very dramatic experience, getting off the planet,” she said. “You’re basically riding a bomb for eight and a half minutes. And then you have the magical experience of being effectively weightless, maneuvering and living and working in zero gravity, which is great, great, great fun. And the view is stupendous.” Her crews’ data collection would seem tedious to outside observers, she said, but on one mission, “we deployed the Hubble Space Telescope.” Many of the people whose signatures appear on the globe had been meaningful to her (Earhart, Walsh, Armstrong, “the whole Apollo 8 crew”); as a kid, she’d admired astronauts and Jacques Cousteau. “These were people living inquisitive and adventurous lives,” she said. “I wanted my life to be like that.” ♦
