A Critic at Large
The Communist Thrillers of Anna Seghers
In her tautly suspenseful novels, fugitives stay one step ahead of the Nazis.
By
Alex Ross
Seghers, in Berlin in 1968. She sketches her characters in a few quick strokes, then subjects them to excruciating tension.Photograph by Roger Melis
“Dante, Dostoyevsky, Kafka—oh, those were bagatelles. Minor inconveniences that blew over,” the German novelist Anna Seghers wrote in late 1940, in a letter from the South of France. “This is serious.” Seghers was one of many German-speaking artists who had sought refuge in France when the Nazis took power, and she was now trying to leave Europe with her family. As a Jewish Communist, she had little chance of survival if she did not get out. But the bureaucratic maze that she had to navigate—obtaining exit visas, transit visas, entrance visas, affidavits, ship bookings—seemed contrived to make escape impossible. Adding to the dark absurdity of the situation was the fact that Seghers’s husband, the Hungarian Marxist scholar László Radványi, was being held in a French internment camp, on the basis that Hungary was a German ally. Finally, in March, 1941, Seghers, Radványi, and their two children boarded the Capitaine Paul Lemerle, bound for Martinique. Other passengers included André Breton, Victor Serge, and Claude Lévi-Strauss—all fleeing the inferno.
Flight was Seghers’s great literary theme. Between 1933 and 1944, she wrote three extraordinary novels that feature young men racing just ahead of the closing jaws of fate. In “Blood Money,” a Communist street fighter hides out in a Nazi-infested village. In “The Seventh Cross,” an escapee from a German concentration camp is the target of a nationwide search. And, in “Transit,” Seghers draws on her own experiences in Marseille in 1940 and 1941, when the grotesque torments of Dostoyevsky and Kafka became mundane reality. She spent the rest of the Second World War in Mexico, then returned to Berlin in 1947. After a few years in the western part of the city, she settled in East Germany, remaining there until her death, in 1983.
Seghers’s Communist affiliations explain the eventual eclipse of her work in the West. “The Seventh Cross” was published in an English translation in 1942 and became a best-seller. A movie adaptation, directed by the Austrian American filmmaker Fred Zinnemann, was released in 1944, with Spencer Tracy in the lead role. During the Cold War, however, Seghers’s work faded from view. For decades, her early books were out of print in English, and her later ones were never translated. After 1989, readers in the former West Germany rediscovered her work, and, in 2013, NYRB Classics began publishing new translations of her novels and stories, including “
The Seventh Cross
” and “
Transit
.” “
Blood Money
” has just been released, meaning that all three of Seghers’s manhunt thrillers are available again.
I use the word “thriller” advisedly. Seghers is not only an unflinching witness of twentieth-century terror; she is also a master of what the blurbers of paperbacks used to call burn-the-midnight-oil suspense. She sketches her characters in a few quick strokes, then subjects them to excruciating tension. Her style is pithy and blunt, avoiding the ornate sentence structure of classical German. She is confident enough of her skill that she sometimes gives away a story’s ending at the start. The uprising will fail. The revolution will sputter out. The ship on which refugees are seeking a berth will sink. What holds us in thrall is the ever-shifting logic—largely cruel, occasionally kind—through which destiny plays itself out.
Seghers was born in 1900 in the ancient Rhineland city of Mainz, as Anna Reiling. At home, she went by Netty. Her father, Isidor, was a well-to-do art-and-antiquities dealer, and her mother, Hedwig, was active in Jewish causes. At first, Seghers leaned toward an academic career, studying art history at Heidelberg University and writing a dissertation on Jewish imagery in Rembrandt. But her relationship with Radványi—a fellow Heidelberg student and a refugee from the Hungarian Revolution of 1918-19—pulled her toward radical politics. She took the pseudonym Seghers from the Dutch painter Hercules Seghers, a contemporary of Rembrandt’s. The name endowed her with a certain mystery—a quality that she cultivated throughout her life. Although she was a vibrant public speaker and a sociable colleague, many found her cagey and elusive. This did not apply to her children, who later marvelled at how she had nurtured them through years of war and exile.
She began publishing fiction in the mid-nineteen-twenties. One of her earliest stories was a wrenching tale titled “Jans Is Going to Die,” about a poor, sickly child who perishes while trying to prove his mettle in games with other boys. (It appears in “
The Dead Girls’ Class Trip
,” an NYRB compilation of Seghers stories.) The scenario is shiveringly bleak, yet Seghers offers compensating moments of fragile beauty, as when Jans looks out his window at a swirl of snowflakes: “He had ten thousand companions every day, these little dancers from somewhere, dancing in courtyards and on windowsills to a music that no one could hear.” In 1928, Seghers published a terse, tense novella entitled “The Revolt of the Fishermen of St. Barbara,” which made her a star of left-wing culture.
Although Seghers was a Communist true believer, the breadth of her literary affinities, from E. T. A. Hoffmann to Kafka, put her in conflict with the dogmas of proletarian fiction. Doctrinaire critics accused her of being bourgeois, formalist, decadent. Indeed, she was never really a realist, even if working-class characters and situations populate her pages. Her settings tend to be a little vague, her protagonists more archetypes than individuals. Following Kafka’s lead, she wrote a series of artfully twisted fables and legends in a style both simple and strange. “The Best Tales of Woynok the Thief,” from 1938, conjures a proud, lonesome bandit whose solitude is tested by a merry company of thieves:
The sound of their songs was as clear and pure as the sound of the organ of Saint Ignaz on that Pentecostal morning when Woynok mixed in among the churchgoers for the first time in order to scout out everything before he set the fire. He had never coveted anything that one couldn’t steal, either by force or by guile, disguised as a pilgrim, or with a foot jammed in the door and the help of a shotgun barrel. He had never known a sorrow that one couldn’t cut or burn out of one’s flesh, or simply shake off like lice. But now, for minutes at a time here, around the fire, there were joys that could not be stolen and sorrows that could not be burned away, for they didn’t even exist.
Even in her more overtly political writing, Seghers retains that errant fairy-tale tone. In her early novel “The Wayfarers,” a story of exiled revolutionaries that has yet to be translated into English, a Bulgarian guerrilla fighter named Dudoff becomes a Woynok-like legend, his escapes from death assuming religious overtones. Communism was, of course, a quasi-religion in its own right, and Seghers saw the need for saviors and martyrs.
“Blood Money,” published in 1933, is Seghers’s first major novel—a seamless blend of journalistic realism and mythic allusion. The opening paragraphs at once apply an iron grip. A farmer named Bastian is coming in from the fields when he buckles over in pain outside his front door. “Close behind him stood Death, its hand raised to add a stone to his load—enough to finish him off,” Seghers writes. Bastian gets up, goes inside, and sits down with his family for dinner. As he is saying the Lord’s Prayer, he hears footsteps coming to the door—“a long shadow was suddenly cast across the twilit parlor.” It is not Death but a fair-haired, blue-eyed twenty-year-old lad named Johann. There’s obviously something amiss with him: he’s sweaty and dirty, he’s wearing someone else’s boots, he’s almost collapsing from hunger. Bastian’s wife surmises that Johann must be a relative, and he is invited to eat. Bastian, in a burst of generosity that he soon regrets, lets the boy spend the night. Seghers coolly adds, “He thought he did so because he believed in God.” The late Margot Bettauer Dembo handled NYRB’s previous Seghers translations; Lucy Jones has taken over, and excellently conveys the incisive bite of the writing.
It is the summer of 1932, and police bulletins are offering a bounty for the capture of Johann, who has been accused of killing a cop during a hunger march in Leipzig. (The novel’s German title, “Der Kopflohn,” means “head price.”) It’s unclear whether Johann is guilty or not, and, given the Nazification of the police, the distinction doesn’t matter. He’s less a shining idealist than an adventurous upstart, his insouciance falling on the line between brave and stupid. He runs errands for a band of local Communists, but he also finds time for a fling with a local girl. His bro-ish ordinariness illustrates the political stakes in 1932—or in any year of your choosing. Seghers shows how the Nazis win over unemployed youth by hosting parades, concerts, and outdoor expeditions. Johann enrages them because, as a model Aryan, he ought to be on their side. Unlike many other leftists, who saw the Nazis as mere puppets of capitalism, Seghers understood the raw, sensual appeal of the Fascist message.
A “Wanted” poster for Johann is hanging in a town near Bastian’s village, and several residents see it. A Jewish merchant named Naphtel is tempted by the reward but feels a “primal aversion, smoldering in honest human hearts, to delivering a persecuted man into the hands of the state.” The downtrodden farmer Algeier could use the money even more, yet he can’t stand the idea that his prosperous neighbor Merz, a zealous Red-hater, would “laugh himself to death to see this boy paraded through the village.” The novel is full of such finely shaded moral studies; no one is completely innocent, with the possible exception of Bastian, a paragon of unquestioning hospitality. Even the hard-core Nazis reveal glints of humanity. A hulking brute named Zillich, whose antisemitic ravings at a political meeting leave other farmers dazed and submissive, loses his menacing aura when he wins prizes at a fairground and exults boyishly.
“Blood Money,” like most of Seghers’s stories, is male-dominated. Scholars of her work have debated why women seldom take center stage. Partly, she may have been yielding to the marketplace: feminism didn’t rank high among leftist concerns. Yet Seghers deftly exposes the insecurity, loneliness, and longing that hide behind masculinist poses. She often suggests a subliminally romantic tie between an older man and a youth, such as the one between Bastian and Johann. Women tend to be victims rather than actors, but they are not rendered mute. The most harrowing scene in “Blood Money” involves a woman named Susann Schüchlin, who is so abused by her husband and so worn down by motherhood that she decides suicide is the only way out. In a scene of terrible power, she drowns herself by jamming her body into a hollow tree trunk through which a stream flows. When, at the end of the novel, Bastian’s niece Sophie marries a wealthy young Nazi, you fear that the same cycle is starting again.
Shortly after the burning of the Reichstag, in February, 1933, Seghers fled Germany and settled in France, where she carried on with up-to-the-minute political storytelling. “The Way Through February” (1935) is a journalistic novel about the Austrian Civil War of 1934, and “The Rescue” (1937) expands on “Blood Money” in showing how Nazi propaganda feeds on the discontents of the German working class. These novels, too, have yet to appear in English, and they may presume too much background knowledge. But the opening sequence of “The Rescue” is another tour de force of coiled action: a stolid working-class hero, trapped in a mine with six comrades, prevents the others from losing hope before rescue arrives.
“I can remember a time when this was all trees.”
Cartoon by Edward Steed
A clammy sensation of entrapment suffuses “The Seventh Cross” (1939), which chronicles the flight across Germany of a fugitive named Georg Heisler. Although Seghers experienced only the first weeks of life in Nazi Germany, she absorbed the accounts of eyewitnesses, including a memoir by the trade unionist Hans Beimler, who had escaped from Dachau in 1933. Seghers’s narrative also eerily anticipates her own frantic maneuvers in Nazi-occupied France. Uncertain about her future, she had sent various manuscripts of the novel abroad. At least one copy fell into the hands of the Gestapo, which was hunting for Seghers and interrogating her associates.
The crosses to which the title alludes are, in fact, plane trees on the grounds of a fictional concentration camp called Westhofen, in southwestern Germany. When seven prisoners break out of the camp, Fahrenberg, the commandant, has the trees shorn of their branches and turned into crosses. Each escapee, upon being caught, is to be crucified. This savage bit of theatre comes back to haunt Fahrenberg when the tree intended for Georg remains unoccupied. The commandant begins to lose sleep fretting over his own survival, and Seghers almost makes us feel sympathy for him. Zillich, the brute from “Blood Money,” reappears as a sadistic guard at Westhofen and becomes the target of Fahrenberg’s panicked fury—one cog in the system getting mangled by another. In a later story, “The End,” set in 1945, Seghers gives her readers the satisfaction of seeing Zillich get his comeuppance, although, as one of his pursuers says, “you can’t kill Satan. You’d have to completely finish off this old, ugly world first.”
Just as Seghers refuses to turn Nazis into cartoon villains, she declines to make her hero a saint. Georg, an unemployed auto mechanic, comes across as an arrogant jock. He picks up Communist ideology from his bookish friend Franz and steals away Franz’s girlfriend in the process. He generally treats women as playthings and casts them aside when they are no longer of use. Men, too, are manipulated. When a male driver gives Georg a ride and shows faint hints of sexual interest, Georg ponders killing him and stealing his car. So why do we care about Georg? Because, as Seghers writes, he has been reduced to the status of a hunted animal, “escaping into the wilderness that was his life.”
Georg, like Johann in “Blood Money,” is a spectral stranger who poses tests for the auxiliary characters. The outcomes are contingent and unpredictable. Consider a teen-ager named Fritz, whose jacket Georg steals. Fritz is inordinately proud of the jacket—a zippered brown corduroy number that he bought to impress his girlfriend. He is an obedient member of the Hitler Youth and seems poised to play the role of the malignant brat. Yet he becomes oddly enamored of his jacket’s outlaw status. When Georg discards the item and it is found by the police, Fritz is summoned to Westhofen to identify it. To his own surprise, he announces that it isn’t his jacket, throwing the search off course. In such trivial moments of rebellion, the seeds of resistance are sown. Heroism is a matter of chance.
Seghers signed a contract for the American edition of “The Seventh Cross” in June, 1941, while she was interned on Ellis Island. She had hoped to gain admission to the United States, but the immigration authorities declared that she and her family could not enter, on the ground that her daughter had “defective vision.” This transparently flimsy excuse covered up the real reason: the F.B.I. had flagged Seghers as a potentially dangerous Communist. J. Edgar Hoover took a personal interest in the case, maintaining surveillance of Seghers once she went to Mexico. Her mail was opened, her friends’ apartments were broken into, copies of “The Seventh Cross” were scrutinized for imaginary codes. Seghers’s F.B.I. file, which eventually ran to nearly a thousand pages, is an ironic boon to scholars, shedding light on her daily life in Mexico and providing insight into the composition process of her masterpiece, “Transit.”
This time, the desperate dude at the center of the story serves as its first-person narrator, which perversely results in our knowing almost nothing about him, not even his real name. He is a disaffected cipher, expertly evoking the agonized chaos of Paris and Marseille in 1940 while remaining ostensibly detached from the proceedings. At times, he sounds like a Raymond Chandler type, revelling in real-life noir. He archly describes, for example, the predicament of a conductor from Prague who has been offered a job leading a spa orchestra in Venezuela:
He had to start the new position in Caracas before the end of the year. He had already had a work contract before and because of the contract, a visa, and because of the visa, a transit visa, but it took so long for the exit visa to be issued that the transit visa expired in the meantime, and after that the visa and after that the contract. Last week he was issued an exit visa, and he was now anxiously waiting for an extension of his contract, which would mean he could then get an extension of his visa. And that would be a prerequisite for his being awarded a new transit visa.
Ultimately, everything falls into place, and the conductor is ready to go—until, at the American consulate, he finds that he has brought only eleven photographs, not the requisite twelve. He loses his booking. Outside, he finds that two of his photos were stuck together. He gets back in line, collapses, and dies. As the narrator watches the ambulance take away the conductor’s body, his mood lifts: “After all I was still young and strong.”
“Transit” bears a resemblance to “Casablanca,” which Seghers possibly saw in Mexico. The principal character puts up a world-weary, hardboiled front, like Humphrey Bogart’s Rick, but over time he melts. When a writer named Weidel kills himself in Paris, leaving behind a suitcase full of manuscripts, the narrator becomes the caretaker of this literary legacy, even though he’s no intellectual. (Seghers modelled Weidel on the Austrian writer Ernst Weiss, who took his life after the fall of Paris. She probably also thought of Walter Benjamin, whose suicide, at the Spanish border, is mentioned in “Transit.”) The protagonist then has an affair with Weidel’s wife, Marie, who thinks that her husband is still alive and searches for him, despite the fact that she is now in love with a third man, a doctor. The intrigue becomes especially heady when the narrator takes over Weidel’s identity. He has a chance to leave on a ship called the Montreal, but he gives up his berth in order to go underground in France. Marie sails away with the doctor. Alas, the first sentence of the novel has foretold their doom: “They’re saying that the Montreal went down between Dakar and Martinique.” It’s like Rick saying to Ilsa, “You’re getting on that plane,” except that the plane crashes.
When our shadowy hero reads Weidel’s unfinished novel, he calls it a fairy tale for adults, about a “wolf who bewitched grown-up children.” He himself is telling a story of that type. It’s a static thriller that unfurls against a deep historical backdrop, with archetypes recurring across time. Seghers observed in a letter that, in Marseille, everyone turns into Odysseus. In the novel, likewise, the narrator assumes an almost Homeric guise, comparing current harbor gossip to chatter from the Phoenician, Cretan, Greek, and Roman eras. He thinks of “mothers who had lost their children, children who had lost their mothers”; he sees “the remnants of crushed armies, escaped slaves, human hordes who had been chased from all the countries of the earth.” A Jewish woman “looks old enough to have been driven out of Vienna not by Hitler but by an edict of the Empress Maria Theresa.” The protagonist becomes a wise-guy version of Benjamin’s Angel of History, watching calamities accumulate before his eyes.
The grim irony hanging over Seghers’s later career is that she fled from one totalitarian state only to become enmeshed in another. Outwardly, she had a position of almost untouchable eminence in the East German cultural apparatus. Between 1952 and 1978, she served as president of the Writers’ Union, functioning as a more or less reliable mouthpiece for Soviet ideology, from Stalin to Brezhnev. Behind the scenes, she shielded colleagues from trouble. Christiane Zehl Romero, her chief biographer, noted that the bullheaded Bertolt Brecht had benefitted from Seghers’s protective maneuvers, as did rebellious younger writers such as Heiner Müller and Christa Wolf. Even as Seghers was hemmed in by fear and uncertainty, she gave no indication that she ever regretted her path. Her story “The Just Judge,” which emerged after the fall of the Wall, tells of an East German judge who refuses to convict an unfairly accused man and is arrested as a result. In prison, the judge is asked whether he would still elect to serve the state if he knew that it would unfairly condemn him. He answers, “I would choose it again, and make this state, just this one, exactly this one, as good as possible.”
After the Second World War, Seghers produced only three more full-length novels, none matching her earlier masterpieces. In 1949, she published “The Dead Stay Young,” a panoramic saga of German revolution and reaction from 1918 to 1945. Although it contains riveting sequences, it tends toward staginess and bagginess, lacking the sweaty momentum of her previous work. “The Decision,” which appeared in 1959, and its sequel, “Trust,” from 1968, dwell laboriously on the reconstitution of the steel industry in an East German town. A sample passage: “They replaced the clay that until then had been used to line the tapping spout with another material that would not be detrimental to the quality of the steel.” Brecht once observed that Seghers thrived on the depiction of oddballs and loners. There are too few of them in the later novels, which answer the official demand for optimistic narratives of rebuilding.
Fortunately, Seghers continued writing shorter fiction, which gave her more leeway to exercise fantasy. (Likewise, Dmitri Shostakovich could experiment more openly in his quartets than in his symphonies.) NYRB’s story collection includes “The Ship of the Argonauts,” an avant-garde fable in which the mythological hero Jason returns from his wanderings and kills time awaiting the fulfillment of his fate. In later years, Seghers wrote several stories set in the Caribbean, one of them dramatizing the Haitian revolutionary Toussaint Louverture. Perhaps NYRB could include these in a second volume of Seghers’s shorter fiction, alongside her late story “Stone Age,” which was inspired by D. B. Cooper, the airplane hijacker who’d parachuted into oblivion in 1971. Seghers transforms Cooper into another of her restless desperadoes—a Vietnam vet in quest of an unspoiled world. The title alludes to General Curtis LeMay’s infamous words about the North Vietnamese: “We’re going to bomb them back into the Stone Age.”
A sovereign observer, Seghers rarely drew directly on her life, but she made an exception in “The Dead Girls’ Class Trip,” a convulsive meditation on the psychic toll of exile. She wrote the story in Mexico in 1943 and 1944, when she was becoming aware that her mother had been killed in the Holocaust. (Her father had died in Mainz in 1940.) The narrator is idling in a rural Mexican village when she hears—or thinks she hears—a voice crying “Netty!” She flashes back to her girlhood in Mainz and, in particular, to a boat trip on the Rhine that she once took with classmates. Memories of the outing are spliced with glimpses of future darkness: Leni will be sent to a concentration camp; Marianne will betray her; Else will die in an air raid; Sophie will be deported, along with their teacher Fräulein Sichel. Yet the day retains its unknowing innocence. Nostalgia and dread meld into one. When Netty returns home, her mother is waiting on a veranda. As Netty begins to climb the stairs, however, the steps stretch out in all directions beneath her, “as infinitely deep as an abyss.” The reverie breaks; the bannister becomes a row of cacti. Still, a hazy thought lingers: Netty never got around to submitting a report on her class trip. She will write it now, although Fräulein Sichel can no longer read it. ♦

By
Ian Buruma
As a film student in Tokyo in the nineteen-seventies, I spent many delightful hours in all-night cinemas watching classic Japanese gangster pictures. These shabby little movie houses, tucked away in the back alleys of Shinjuku, smelled of urine and stale tobacco. The cigarette-burned seats were occupied not only by hard-core yakuza-film enthusiasts but also by scruffy men in search of shelter for the night who snored loudly throughout a succession of violent pictures.
The classic gangster films, mostly made by the Toei studio in the nineteen-sixties, starred such specialists in the yakuza genre as Takakura Ken—Ken-san to his many fans—and followed a simple formula. The bad yakuza were capitalist mobsters in pin-striped suits who fought with guns and were closely linked to crooked businessmen and corrupt officials. The good yakuza wore kimonos, fought with samurai swords, and were traditionalists who were driven by the demands of
giri
and
ninjo:
obligation and humanity. To avenge an injustice and restore honor, a good yakuza, like Ken-san, would set off alone for a suicidal last stand against his wicked rivals. This climactic scene could even rouse some of the sleepers, who would shout lustily at the screen, “Time to die!”
The all-night cinemas were a holdover from the nineteen-fifties and sixties. And the movies showed a world that had long ceased to exist, if it ever had. Violent and predictable, they offered fantasies of a traditional Japan that stood in stark contrast to the neon-lit concrete jungle of contemporary Tokyo, where real yakuza made their money through extortion, prostitution, gunrunning, and blackmail. The trope of the outlaw as a man of honor can be found across the world, of course, but the Japanese version is particularly given to nostalgia. The yakuza movies of the nineteen-sixties have more in common with classic Westerns than with American gangster flicks. John Wayne and Gary Cooper, like Ken-san, often played anachronistic loners from a disappearing Arcadia that was being destroyed by hard-nosed modernizers—greedy bankers, railway owners, big-city politicians. In Japan, perhaps even more than in the American West, the mythology of the outlaw owes much to the extraordinary speed of social and economic change.
What We’re Reading
Discover notable new fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.
Over the past century, the yakuza and the cinema that helped shape their self-image have been tightly linked. In the nineteen-twenties, a mob boss played outlaws in silent films, and later some mobsters became movie stars by playing such roles. Toei had close ties to the Yamaguchi-gumi, the biggest gang in Japan; in the early seventies, the syndicate boss’s son helped make a series of hagiographic films about his father—played by Ken-san. Actual criminals would, in turn, mimic the styles of fantasy gangsters in the movies.
The dream of the traditionalist outlaw fighting for justice is much older than the movies. As Andrew Rankin observes in his gripping new book, “
Yakuza: A 400-Year History of the Japanese Underworld
” (Basic), “Japanese gangsters have spent the past few centuries fashioning an
image
based on warrior culture, while
pretending
to uphold a code of chivalry and honor.”
Rankin traces the myth all the way back to around 100 B.C.E., when Sima Qian, the first great Chinese historian, wrote about highway robbers who did “their utmost to honor any agreement they have made, all without the slightest concern for their own safety.” Even more influential in shaping the Japanese-mobster style was “
Water Margin
,” a fourteenth-century Chinese novel about twelfth-century bandit heroes who robbed the rich and protected the common people against venal and oppressive officials.
Rankin’s study of the Japanese underworld really begins in the early seventeenth century. The Tokugawa shogunate had brought a period of civil wars to an end, and during the long, uninterrupted peace under its iron rule there were fewer opportunities for men who had been trained to fight. Many samurai became bureaucrats. Only criminals still made a living from violence. Déclassé warriors, sometimes joined by street toughs from other walks of life, gave themselves the airs of swashbuckling samurai. It was then that, in Rankin’s words, “some elements of Japan’s popular culture began to look for models of heroism, loyalty, and self-sacrifice in outlaws or people living on the edge of the criminal world.” Gamblers, robbers, and firefighters provided the glamour of derring-do in a pacified and increasingly mercantile society.
Much of what later became known as Bushido, the way of the warrior, was also developed in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The most famous Bushido text, “
Hagakure
” (“The Book of the Samurai”), written in the early eighteenth century by a samurai turned clerk, prescribed ideals of honorable warrior conduct in minute detail. But this was really a form of dandyism, of theatre—a bit like jousting in Europe during the late Middle Ages, when combat between knights had become a performance of chivalry.
Although Japanese versions of the classic Chinese outlaw tales had circulated since the eighteenth century, the images that proved most influential appeared in the early nineteenth, when artists such as Utagawa Kuniyoshi made prints depicting these Robin Hood figures with intricate full-body tattoos. The prints helped set off a tattoo craze, and the style they popularized became closely associated with Japan’s criminal underworld. Some gangsters still wear elaborate designs all over their bodies, and the association with the yakuza remains strong enough that most public baths, swimming pools, and saunas in Japan shun tattooed customers. (That can create complications when Japan hosts international sporting events and tattooed athletes and fans arrive from abroad.)
As Japan entered a period of political upheaval in the mid-nineteenth century, criminal gangs became useful in a new way. In 1854, the U.S. fleet, under Commodore Matthew Perry, had forced the Japanese to open their ports to foreign ships, exposing Japan’s vulnerability. The panicked Japanese élites divided broadly into three camps: those who would appease the foreigners and submit to the unequal treaties; those who would fight the barbarians to the death; and those who would keep the foreigners at bay while modernizing the nation to resist further encroachments. The shogunate’s government chose appeasement. Radicals, outraged at its concessions, wanted to fight and topple the shogunate in favor of imperial rule. Reformers played for time. It was then that the Tokugawa rulers asked criminal gangs to fight the radicals on their behalf.
The alliance was an early instance of a pattern that would recur any time Japan entered a period of political or economic turbulence. Whenever the power of the state is weakened, Rankin writes, political leaders invite the yakuza bosses “to emerge from the underworld and cooperate openly with agents of the state to control unruly or subversive elements.” Relations between criminals and the authorities would become especially cozy; nostalgic references to a lost past would provide a false sense of continuity.
That history of coöperation has helped give Japanese crime its distinctive form. Petty street crime has long been quite rare, in part because criminal enterprise tends to be highly organized. As was often said of New York neighborhoods with a strong Mafia presence, tightly run hierarchical mobs like to control the streets, and have little use for violent freelancers. In Japan, this has meant not only a great deal of collusion between yakuza gangs and law enforcement but also considerable overlap between crime and politics—especially, though not exclusively, right-wing politics. None of this is unique to Japan, but it is particularly conspicuous there.
In the nineteen-seventies, I interviewed a yakuza boss, a courteous man who handed me his card, with the name of his gang embossed in gold. A rather flashy calligraphic rendering of the Chinese character for “sincerity” hung on the wall of his establishment. Green tea was served by gang members shuffling around in slippers. I noticed another guest sipping his tea. He didn’t say much, but nodded politely when the boss held forth to me about chivalry, loyalty, and ancient warrior codes. The quiet man was later introduced to me as the local police chief.
The scene was a modern echo of the old accommodation between gangsters and the state. But the criminal auxiliaries enlisted by the Tokugawa rulers were fighting for a lost cause. The shogunate fell in the Meiji Restoration of 1868. The emperor was installed in Tokyo as the absolute ruler (on paper, at least), and Japan modernized at breakneck speed. The old caste system that privileged the samurai was abolished. Japanese élites dressed in European fashions and adopted Western manners: ballroom dancing, meat eating, attending classical-music concerts, and so on. Big business and industry thrived. Rapid change and Western influence gave the yakuza all the more reason, as Rankin observes, to “cultivate a nostalgic image of themselves as upholders of old feudal ways.”
But the modernizing economy also provided organized crime with new opportunities. No longer confined to gambling dens and brothel districts, yakuza muscled their way into other businesses, some legal, some not. Among the new rackets were providing cheap workers to new industries, ruling the docks of large port cities, extorting money from trading companies, and working for political parties to intimidate rival voters. By the eighteen-nineties, crime had taken on an international dimension as Japan expanded its empire overseas and yakuza trafficked young Japanese women to brothel owners in China and Southeast Asia.
To burnish the public image and the self-image of men engaged in such sordid enterprises, all kinds of pseudo-traditional rituals and ceremonies were revived or invented. Lapses in yakuza discipline were atoned for by offering the offended party one of the offender’s fingers, wrapped in silk cloth. The funerals of yakuza bosses were highly formal affairs, often attended by politicians and business leaders. In a way, the ruthless modernity of criminal enterprise demanded a new veneer of invented tradition. This is why many classic yakuza movies are set in the late nineteenth century, when the contrast between bad guys in business suits and good guys in kimonos offered rich dramatic possibilities.
Yakuza gangs also burnished their reputation by helping ordinary citizens with problems that the authorities couldn’t or didn’t wish to handle. Local disputes were adjudicated. Loans were offered when banks refused. Businesses were protected against rival criminal predators. When democratic activists demanded greater civil rights in the late nineteenth century, some yakuza came out to guard their rallies.
“Call it a midlife crisis, but I’ve decided not to swim upstream and die.”
Cartoon by Rose Anne Prevec
But protection and help from gangsters usually have a steep price. And the idea that yakuza were on the side of the common man was rarely anything more than a pretense. They were of far greater help to powerful political and business interests. Like criminal organizations everywhere, yakuza tend to be conservative. When citizens rioted in 1918 because the prices of essential commodities such as rice had spiralled out of control, gangsters were hired to crack down on the protesters. They were also recruited to put down industrial strikes and to lean on union organizers.
The reactionary spirit of mobsters was particularly useful to the authorities when left-wing politics gained steam in the aftermath of the Russian Revolution. Yakuza organized ultra-nationalist outfits like the National Essence Society, which aimed to crush such noxious foreign influences as Marxism. A number of yakuza bosses even entered parliament. One of them got his start with money borrowed from his sister’s brothel. Another, Koizumi Matajiro, who sported a red-dragon tattoo on his back, had made his name as a tough guy in the dock yards of a naval base. (His grandson Koizumi Junichiro was Prime Minister from 2001 to 2006.)
In the nineteen-thirties—a decade of political assassinations, failed military coups, brutal invasions of China, and a hard-right reaction against the relative liberalism of the nineteen-twenties—the yakuza embraced the Zeitgeist with gusto. Political extremism and organized crime became increasingly entangled. Rankin singles out the remarkable career of Sakai Eizo, a racketeer who founded the Great Japanese Order of Righteousness. Sakai hired out his men to break strikes with violence, which was par for the course in his line of business. Less usual was his infatuation with Mussolini’s Blackshirts, whose uniform he adapted for his own gang. Between the wars, Sakai travelled to Rome multiple times to meet his hero. Rankin writes that he presented Il Duce with a suit of samurai armor, pledging an “eternal spiritual partnership” with the Italian Fascists. In Berlin, surrounded by grinning Storm Troopers, he briefly met Heinrich Himmler.
The Second World War was not a fruitful time for the yakuza. Brothels were closed, and few people had enough money to gamble. The economy was now under military control. Some gangs went out of business, and several mob bosses lost their fortunes. Rankin points to a character named Chubby Shino, whose “henchmen learned of his impoverishment only when they attended his funeral, and the discovery was said to have caused them much embarrassment and shame.”
Rankin has less to say about the shadowy criminal entrepreneurs who flourished in occupied China and Japanese-ruled Manchuria. Their rackets—plunder, opium trafficking, and much else—were often run not by members of established yakuza gangs but by fixers and political operators who exploited their connections with the Imperial Japanese Army. But Rankin does mention a thuggish figure named Kodama Yoshio, who worked for Japanese spy agencies in China while trading in narcotics and smuggled goods. After the war, Kodama was detained by the American occupation authorities as a suspected Class A war criminal, though he was released without trial. He later used his wartime connections to serve as a broker between yakuza gangs and right-wing politicians, while also serving as a C.I.A. asset. (A bribery scandal in the nineteen-seventies involving Prime Minister Tanaka Kakuei and the Lockheed Corporation brought his colorful career to an end.)
Kodama was closely associated with an equally shady character named Sasakawa Ryoichi, who also made a great deal of money in occupied China and operated in the same postwar twilight world of officialdom, right-wing agitation, and organized crime. Sasakawa, like Sakai, was a great admirer of Mussolini, and formed the extreme right-wing Patriotic People’s Party. He, too, was imprisoned as a suspected Class A war criminal, and he liked to boast that he was “the world’s richest fascist.” After his release, he added to his fortune by turning motorboat racing into a betting enterprise. Sasakawa didn’t pretend to be a modern-day samurai. Instead, he promoted himself as a philanthropist, donating money to all kinds of causes, some of them worthy, in the hope of receiving the Nobel Peace Prize. The prize eluded him, but there is a bust of Sasakawa at the World Health Organization, in Geneva.
The decades after Japan’s defeat were a golden age for the yakuza. Cities almost entirely destroyed by American bombs had to be rebuilt. Black markets catered to the needs of a desperate population, charging extortionate prices. Guns looted from Japanese and U.S. military supplies were plentiful. Women, poor and often single because so many men had died in the war, turned to prostitution in large numbers; some, known as
panpan
girls, catered to American G.I.s, while others served local men. There was a lucrative trade in
hiropon
, a brand of methamphetamine. And many battle-hardened, unemployed veterans meant that there were fresh recruits for the yakuza gangs.
The late nineteen-forties provided another favorite setting for classic yakuza films. The mythical image of the chivalrous mobster offered a way to ease the humiliating memory of losing the war and carried a nationalist charge, exploited in movies set amid black markets, rapacious Americans, and
panpan
girls. In the previous decades, Japan had brought in many Korean, Chinese, and Taiwanese laborers, often under duress, to work in factories and mines, usually in atrocious conditions. Many went home when the war was over, but many did not. They formed criminal gangs that fought Japanese mobsters for control of the bomb-cratered streets. In the exaggerated version of history promoted by yakuza movies of the nineteen-sixties, Korean and Taiwanese gangsters enjoyed the protection of the American occupation government. Onscreen, this ethnic conflict allowed Ken-san and other kimonoed gangsters to be presented as pure, sincere, patriotic heroes fighting for traditional Japanese values against savage aliens as well as local, gun-toting yakuza. The politics of these entertainments reflected those of the right-wing, crime-riddled organizations of prewar and wartime Japan—highly chauvinistic, hierarchical, and hostile to Western-style modernity.
In real life, the yakuza gangs were not always so xenophobic. Most crime syndicates were more welcoming to Korean recruits, for example, than mainstream corporations were. Members of the traditional outcast community, the Burakumin, who engaged in trades that Buddhists consider polluted, such as animal slaughter, were also heavily represented in yakuza gangs—so much so that political organizations standing up for outcast rights were often mobbed up. (Dominating the meat business was a highly lucrative enterprise, though that wasn’t an aspect of yakuza life that the movies showed.) At the same time, politicians and business leaders still employed yakuza for various tasks in mid-century Japan. When plans were made for a visit to Japan by President Eisenhower in 1960—it was eventually called off—there weren’t enough policemen to guard his route into Tokyo, so the yakuza were mobilized to help.
Despite the reactionary politics of the yakuza films, not to mention of the syndicates themselves, Ken-san was very popular among left-wing student protesters in the late nineteen-sixties. What could the antiwar students possibly have had in common with an anachronistic yakuza hero? Well, like the alienated yakuza loner, they hated the corrupt politicians and shady businessmen driving the economic boom. Above all, the protesters resented U.S. domination of postwar Japanese politics and culture, especially during the Vietnam War. The fact that they themselves benefitted from Japan’s booming economy and were deeply influenced by American culture only sharpened their resentments. The idea of crashing into the modern office of a capitalist gang with nothing but a samurai sword and a sense of moral righteousness had a certain romantic appeal.
In some instances, student radicalism spilled over into yakuza activities. I once met a man who had been a protest leader at the University of Tokyo in the sixties and was now working for the yakuza by digging up dirt on corporations, which his bosses used to blackmail them. He claimed that he and the yakuza were on the same side. A more public version of this racket was played out at shareholder meetings. Racketeers blackmailed companies and executives, threatened to disrupt shareholder meetings, or intimidated other shareholders to keep quiet. These extortionists, called
sōkaiya
, were frequently connected to extreme right-wing groups whose younger members would speed around town in trucks festooned with rising-sun flags and military regalia, blaring wartime marches through powerful loudspeakers.
After the nineteen-sixties, though, the image of Japanese gangsters began to change. Men of honor, with full-body tattoos and missing fingers, exchanging sake cups in elaborate brotherhood rituals, were becoming a bit passé, even as a fantasy. Yakuza movies kept pace. A new type of gangster picture emerged in the nineteen-seventies, edgy and hardboiled, with such titles as “Battles Without Honor and Humanity” (1973) and “Graveyard of Honor” (1975). Postwar Hiroshima was a popular setting for these movie gangsters, who fought dirty, had no use for the old ceremonies, and wore flashy suits and aviator shades. Hiroshima was, in fact, especially notorious for its criminal gangs, probably because its near-total destruction had disrupted civilian life with particular severity.
This new type of yakuza movie often featured over-the-top violence, but its depiction of the criminal underworld was more realistic than that of the classic movies I watched in the all-night cinemas. The moral distinctions among mainstream business, the yakuza gangs, and the police were often blurry. This cynical, even nihilistic attitude reflected changes in real life.
But the older image of the yakuza as protectors of the community did not disappear altogether. When Kobe, home of the Yamaguchi-gumi, was devastated by an earthquake in 1995, yakuza provided food and supplies from the parking lot of their headquarters. Beginning in 1991, however, tougher laws severely restricted the gangs’ activities and their dealings with legitimate businesses.
Rankin plausibly argues that these laws, together with the gradual exclusion of the yakuza from their old domains in entertainment, finance, and the property business, changed the nature of crime in Japan. The yakuza syndicates had a choice: they could either “cease engaging in predatory crimes targeting civilians” or “become fully criminal clandestine groups like mafias and wage war against the authorities.” “Most gangs,” he adds, “prudently took the first option.”
Of course, crime didn’t just disappear. There is still an underground economy in drugs (especially methamphetamine) and gun smuggling, and the yakuza retain a strong interest in the sex trade. But Japanese gangs now face new competition. In recent decades, Japan has become a more cosmopolitan country, with a growing immigrant population and, inevitably, some imported crime. In Tokyo and Osaka, there are Chinese gangsters, Brazilian robbers, and even a gang of thieves from Serbia and Montenegro called the Pink Panthers. As Rankin puts it, crime in Japan is “being invigorated by cultural diversity.” The newcomers have stirred up some of the same fears and prejudices that fuelled movies set in the aftermath of the Second World War. Panic about predatory outsiders is, of course, grist for the mill of right-wing populists, including the very conservative current Prime Minister, Takaichi Sanae.
No wonder, then, that members of some old syndicates now seek credit for barring such foreigners from their ranks, as though the yakuza were still defenders of a noble Japanese tradition. But Rankin mentions a Japanese mobster who was asked what the arrival of overseas competitors meant for the ancient codes of yakuza chivalry. “Rules aren’t worth shit nowadays,” he replied. “Mafias from other countries are moving into Japan. If we stick with tradition, they’ll take over all of our business.” Ken-san, my old hero, must be rolling in his grave. ♦

The Art World
Deana Lawson’s Subjects of Surveillance
In a new series featuring security-camera stills of suspected shoplifters, the photographer seems more interested in the surface than in the soul.
By
Hilton Als
“Edge Control edvc,” 2023. For the series, Lawson shot a number of “walls of shame” in beauty-supply stores, where surveillance-camera stills of suspected shoplifters are posted.Photograph by Deana Lawson / Courtesy the artist / Gagosian
For some days before and after I saw the photography-based artist Deana Lawson’s current exhibition at Gagosian (through October 24th), I read and reread John Szarkowski’s majestic and liberating 1966 book, “The Photographer’s Eye,” to remind myself of what’s fascinated me about the medium from the beginning. As the director of photography at the Museum of Modern Art from 1962 to 1991, Szarkowski organized complex exhibitions—now seen as historic—featuring the work of then relatively unknown artists such as Eugène Atget and Diane Arbus, photographers who illuminated the real and the fantastic in the mysterious modern world. “The Photographer’s Eye” sits in the hand like a family album. Its black-and-white photographs and minimal text are divided into sections: “The Thing Itself,” “The Detail,” “The Frame,” “Time,” and “Vantage Point.” Szarkowski doesn’t shy away from discussing photography’s limitations—it’s a time-based art, restricted to the facts of the moment—but also celebrates all the wonders that can happen within the frame. He draws a useful comparison between photographers and the Old Master painters Paolo Uccello and Diego Velázquez. Whereas those painters combined “elements which had been separate in space and time” to create a composite picture about military power and war, Szarkowski writes, photographers who shoot outside the studio can’t stage-manage in that way. “From the reality before him,” Szarkowski says, the photographer “could only choose that part that seemed relevant and consistent.” Denied the power of narrative, the photographer has to focus on the symbol or the “significant detail” to tell a story, while letting the image contain ambiguity, too. What could that dirt road and the horizon beyond it mean—hope or hopelessness? And what do that soldier’s eyes reveal as he looks out at us from Korea in 1950? Is he weary, or wary, or poised for battle? Szarkowski makes a number of other vital points in the book, chief among them that photography as a phenomenon belongs not just to the artist but to anyone with vision. This beautifully egalitarian perspective helped democratize the medium, allowing everyone a chance to look and to see. But it didn’t necessarily help the art market, or the role that creators like Lawson play in it.
Lawson, now forty-seven, first became widely known in the twenty-tens, when her work was shown in the
MOMA
’s “New Photography 2011,” and in “Ruffneck Constructivists” (curated by the artist Kara Walker), at the Institute of Contemporary Art in Philadelphia, in 2014. Lawson’s large-scale color pictures in those shows were, like much of her work, staged shots, in which Black figures were presented in heightened, theatrical contexts. Born in 1979 into a Black working-class family in Rochester, New York, Lawson, whose mother was an administrative assistant at Kodak and whose father was an amateur photographer, studied photography at Penn State and at the Rhode Island School of Design. Arbus was among the photographers she grew up admiring, and Arbus’s stunning “Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey, 1966” likely had a considerable influence on “Roxie and Raquel, New Orleans, Louisiana” (2010), the first work of Lawson’s that I remember seeing.
Marianne Wex. Panels from “Let’s Take Back Our Space: ‘Female’ and ‘Male’ Body Language as a Result of Patriarchal Structures,” 1977.Photograph by Marianne Wex / Courtesy Marianne Wex Estate / MOMA
In “Roxie and Raquel,” two young women of color—twins—kneel at the center of a mattress, their backs to each other, heads turned to face the camera. Each has one hand on her thigh and the other arm raised above her head, fingers touching her sister’s. (I learned later that Lawson herself is a twin.) What distinguishes the two women at first glance is their clothing: the sister on the left wears a gold tank top and gold high heels, while the one on the right has a modest white blouse under a sweater vest—sartorial versions of Toni Morrison’s Sula and Nel. Once you’ve taken in the twins’ outfits, you focus on their eyes; one sister looks sadder than the other. To this study of contrasts and sameness—the high-heeled sister, whose attire indicates that she wants to be looked at, is “bad,” whereas her twin represents modesty and goodness—Lawson adds a kind of sexual melancholy: Which woman will be desired in the world? Which will become a forgotten understudy in the theatre of life? Who will love them? Love is the ultimate ambiguity.
In the late nineteen-seventies, the art critic and curator Douglas Crimp dubbed the young artists Cindy Sherman, Laurie Simmons, Sherrie Levine, and Louise Lawler, among others, the “Pictures Generation”—artists making work that offered a critique of gender and of the notion of originality (and, thus, of Szarkowski’s view of the photographer as auteur). Alienation, role-playing, commercial impulses—these creators explored all of these things as they made Marxism visual. Political stratagems in art were shifting in places like New York and Los Angeles, and the Pictures Generation’s ethos began to speak to young Black and brown artists, ultimately intersecting with their desire for representation. Slowly but definitely, the “other” aesthetic made inroads into the formerly largely white and male art world and art market. These new and alternative visions were being seen because they were now part of the economy of art, and the stories that Lawson told, and wanted to tell, in her early works, like “Roxie and Raquel” or “Mickey and Friends” (2010)—in which two nude women, one dark-skinned and one lighter, stand facing each other, each with a hand on the other’s hip, below a mural of a delighted Mickey Mouse holding an ice-cream cone—showed how much photography and the market for it had changed in the preceding decades.
Still, I found it difficult to see beneath the surface of those early photographs of Lawson’s. Did the work borrow from Surrealism, from Claude Cahun’s and Hans Bellmer’s staged photographs exploring play, sex, and identity? And, if so, where was the mystery that I was accustomed to seeing in those older (and, yes, European) artists’ work? In the end, for me, looking at Lawson’s early pieces was like listening to Mary J. Blige trying to sing in Chaka Khan’s register: she was flat. And what she was showing us, with her many oiled-up—if not greasy, and thus “funky”—bodies (Lawson doesn’t do anything as plebeian and real as “ashy”), was a testament not to a vision but to the power of the internalized white gaze.
The Gagosian show features seventeen photographs from a series that Lawson began in 2023, titled “Edge Control”—for a popular beauty product that smooths out the baby hairs along women’s hairlines and is one of the most frequently stolen items from beauty-supply stores. “Edge Control” is inspired in part by Jonathan Crary’s 2022 book “Scorched Earth: Beyond the Digital Age to a Post-Capitalist World” and also draws on Philip K. Dick’s novel “A Scanner Darkly,” a dystopian tale from 1977 that is full of mad poetry and brilliant imagery. At its center is a youngish man named Bob Arctor, an undercover cop who starts using drugs in order to infiltrate a house full of addicts in Southern California. At a certain point, he becomes addicted to Substance D, or “Slow Death,” a powerful psychoactive drug, and then other things happen to heighten his sense that the world and his body are one, and that both are being secretly spied on. It’s on the idea of surveillance that “Edge Control” hangs its theoretical hat, and the beauty product here is the addictive substance. Is beauty worth stealing?
Can
you steal it?
A fair number of the people we see in this series are Black women. The images are photographs of photographs: Lawson shot “walls of shame” in beauty-supply stores, where surveillance-camera stills of suspected shoplifters are posted. The original pictures are low quality—at once smeary, ominous, and mundane. They’re artifacts from a place we recognize but don’t want to inhabit, part of Lawson’s sleaze aesthetic. At the same time, the works are all handsomely printed and framed with black mirrors. Lawson has said that she hoped the frames would make the photographs seem “like jewels,” and would make the women depicted proud if they ever saw the works. But the framing also underlines the difference between the presentation of the images and the presumed impoverishment of their subjects: money trumps poverty every time.
At times, I felt queasy looking at these pictures, in part because Lawson doesn’t ask us to take her subjects in. All is alienation and bright colors—even when blurred. Lawson’s ostensible thieves have the look of zombies. Their interiority is not the point; apply enough political theory and you lose sight of the human—something Arbus never did. Arbus used the “odd” as a way in; Lawson stops at the door. She seems more interested in the subject’s surface than in the soul. I kept going back to “Edge Control,” trying not to see race as a kind of prop—an excuse for the agitprop—in the work. Do we mirror the society we’ve made? All those skulking people in harshly lit aisles looking for the transformative power of beauty that they can’t afford? Or is Lawson primarily interested in making a commodifiable object, in which the subject is raw, down, but is viewed from an attractively framed distance?
The question of photography and surveillance is, if not an old one, certainly a familiar one. (These themes were explored in the Tate Modern’s important 2010 show “Exposed: Voyeurism, Surveillance and the Camera” and, in 2018, in the Met’s “Everything Is Connected,” about art, surveillance, and conspiracy.) The second time I went to Gagosian to see “Edge Control,” I remembered some color photographs that Nick Knight took of Kate Moss for
Vogue
in 1995. Moss, styled by Camilla Nickerson, appears in various pristine white outfits and is shot as though from a surveillance camera; the images look slightly blasted out, cold. This is a sleek world, and Moss is makeup-ready, but you feel something for the woman she portrays in the images: she is isolated, standing in an elevator, sitting behind the wheel of a car, walking down a city street, all in a world mysteriously devoid of other people. She’s alone with all her marketable beauty; only Big Brother is watching her, is watching us now. In fact, Moss’s lonely woman may be one of the reasons someone would want to steal Edge Control in the first place—to look like a commodified object. This is a powerful dream. Remember that moment in Jennie Livingston’s extraordinary documentary “Paris Is Burning” (1990), when the trans woman Octavia St. Laurent shows up at an open call to be a Ford model? Every baby hair is in place; she loves the clothes and the fantasy that magazines promote; she knows that she belongs in that world. But her fantasy can’t break through the reality of her race and the fact that she’s trans. Her dreams exist in opposition to a marketplace where she does not fit. And when has the poor individual ever beat out capital?
One woman in the “Edge Control” series wears an affirming T-shirt that says “Self Love Club,” but how can she be self-loving in a world that identifies her—because of her race and her poverty and her gender—as a presumed thief? I wonder if the women in “Edge Control” are actually used to being surveilled, because of their poverty. Is surveillance supposed to protect “us” from “them”? To protect the haves from the have-nots, with all their awful need, not just in beauty-supply shops but wherever those destitute monsters threaten our world of health and prosperity with their raggedy wigs and clothing and their covert, thieving behavior? The narratives of the people in “Edge Control” don’t move beyond the picture frame; Lawson fails to present significant details that might—as Szarkowski suggests—tell us more about this or that moment, this or that person. Instead, the works in “Edge Control,” despite the pain of the racism depicted, are two-dimensional documents in which Black people, the poor, and women are targeted, and then what? So what? Lawson’s idea runs out of steam early on in the series, because it’s less an idea than a trope stuck to a pretty piece of paper.
It’s not that the artist Marianne Wex has any answers about the gendered body, but, boy, does she take the question and run with it. In her brilliant 1972-77 photographic series “Let’s Take Back Our Space: ‘Female’ and ‘Male’ Body Language as a Result of Patriarchal Structures”—which is the standout work in “Taking Back Our Space: Photographic Perspectives” (at
MoMa
, through May 2nd)—gestures say so much, and women, in particular, physically mimic power without questioning its source. Wex was a young painter, living in Germany and working at the same time as the Pictures Generation, when she created the series. She didn’t consider herself a photographer, but she wanted to document what was happening to her body, and why. In an interview with the curators Roxana Marcoci and Madeline Weisburg, Wex says, about the genesis of the work, “I didn’t know why I sat so tight, so constricted, even when I was alone. This led me to want to see how other women occupied their space in the world.”
Using a Japanese medium-format Mamiya camera, Wex went out looking for herself and found a universe of sick bodies—bodies made ill by the patriarchy and by poverty. She would mount her small black-and-white prints on boards and write brief captions for them. On one board, with the caption “Sitting Arms,” we see, in the upper right-hand corner, a man and a woman in bright sunlight on a park bench. The man is reclining, his arms resting on the back of the bench, while the woman sits upright, with her legs and arms crossed. Below that image are five photographs featuring men, each sitting in a way that suggests repose. The next row shows a series of women who are not so relaxed. Indeed, they are all posing for the photographer, their hands held close to or around their face or neck. If the camera is male, or an instrument of power—and it is—these women have been trained to make themselves “feminine” for it.
On the two boards that make up “Possessive Holds,” Wex makes you see something else. Guys rest their arms on girls’ shoulders while looking straight at the camera, as if to say,
Mine
. I know these pictures to be true because, without exception, when I walk alone on the streets of New York, if a white man spies me—and all I represent to him—approaching, and his girl seems unaware of the imminent threat, he makes sure to take her arm and claim her quickly.
Mine
. But to whom do the women in Lawson’s pictures belong? I’m not entirely sure that she views them as anything more than objects of otherness. They seem framed less by the camera than by the photographer, made “real” by Lawson’s desire to convey menace, socioeconomic disadvantage: the funk of Black life.
Lawson doesn’t want to eliminate Szarkowski’s view of photography as much as she wants to render it outdated, trivial. The world that she presents here is not a new Black Eden but a beaten-down community, familiar to the white man within. The Gagosian show includes works that aren’t part of “Edge Control,” a number of sad, lost pictures that bear no direct relationship to the isolation or to the world of fashion that Knight’s Kate Moss inhabited, though they do reflect a trend in art. In “Baby Throne” (2025), for instance, we see a young Black woman, with swollen legs, nursing a baby at her oversized breast. The mother’s white bra straps and red dress are part of the landscape of color in the living rooms and bedrooms where Lawson finds her images. Here, the walls are yellow, as is the fabric covering of the couch that the woman is sitting on; to the left of the frame, we see the white knitted cover of another piece of furniture, with a white Teddy bear resting on it. This young mother is a child holding a child. She is also an object of political fascination—the underprivileged as spectacle—while the knitting and the Teddy bear call to mind hip art, like the Mike Kelley-inspired fantasy world that Precious Okoyomon puts forth in her installations. One feels anguish while looking at “Baby Throne” because of what Lawson leaves out (what Alice Neel, for instance, has full command of in her extraordinary 1972 portrait of a mother and her disabled child, “Carmen and Judy”): reciprocal emotion. Would any of these images work without their signifier-heavy settings and props? Lawson’s world may read as Black, but in the end it’s the kind of Blackness that any white person can readily understand—and commodify. ♦

The Theatre
“Degenerates” Is Funny, Pervy, and Startling
Else Went’s new play dares to display some empathy for the troubled denizens of the manosphere.
By
Emily Nussbaum
Else Went’s propulsive repartee replicates the twisted energy of a chat room at 3 A.M.Illustration by Jim Stoten
Else Went’s electrifying new play, “Degenerates,” at Playwrights Horizons, begins in darkness, with the audience eavesdropping on an anguished call to a suicide hotline. The caller, a trembling, panicky young man named Kemp, insists, between bouts of paranoia—is the operator an A.I.?—that he is fated to be alone, unloved, and unlovable. He is a “half person” in society’s eyes. Kemp can’t share his feelings with his parents, who don’t get how much the world has changed. When he “tried IRL,” by confiding in his co-workers, they froze him out. “People hate seeing men in pain,” he says, bitterly. There’s one exception in his life, he acknowledges, with a despairing laugh: “Yeah, I know a guy. He’s gonna love hearing about this.”
This sequence is the first in a set of shrewd structural gambits, a forced baptism in empathy for an incel—the sort of man who is generally portrayed in art as a loser at best, a monster at worst. But if that heartrending hotline exchange suggests that Went’s play—which is skillfully directed by her spouse, Emma Rosa Went—will go easy on the troubled denizens of the manosphere, the mood shifts when the lights come up to show Miller, the secret sharer Kemp mentioned. The self-appointed leader of a Discord support group, Miller (Zachary Desmond, crackling with venom) is mid-rant, spitting bile about “this little nine-year-old cunt” from his elementary school—a fourth-grade girl he calls a “heifer” and a “femoid.” Chiming in with support on an audio feed are his followers: Kemp, twenty-one, the sad sack from the hotline; Target, a fey, agoraphobic eighteen-year-old anime fan who earns a living online as a niche streamer; and Serge, thirty-three, a combative newcomer. The stage is split in two: on the left, outlined in pale green, is Miller’s spartan lair, with a microwave, a Smiths poster, and dirty laundry. On the right, bathed in neon pink, is Target’s place, a blitzkrieg of manga imagery, the walls covered in posters of girl warriors with marshmallow bosoms.
What follows is a delirious, unpredictable theatrical experience, which begins as anthropology and then unveils itself as something more provocative: an exploration of the possibilities and limits of human intimacy. For a while, Miller’s followers shoot the shit with their nastily charismatic guru, sharing their experiences of rejection and sparring over racist jabs disguised as jokes (then justified as science). They share links to the profiles of women who rejected them, then rate their looks. There’s a particularly frightening moment when Miller finds his “heifer” classmate online and discovers that she’s become a post-top-surgery queer progressive with short hair and a social-media display adorned with Ukrainian flags and Black Lives Matter slogans. “Have at her,” he sneers. “Full-blown fucking bluehair uwu enby feminist freak.” The dialogue is often like this, a riotous, disorienting, and sometimes horrifying thicket of the cryptic argot—“hypergamy,” “mewing”—that is the Esperanto of the terminally online. When Miller dismissed one man as “MGTOW” (pronounced “mig-tau”), I nodded, sagely. Oh, yes, the shorthand for “men going their own way,” the red-pilled cadre who reject women, as opposed to incels (“involuntary celibates”), who feel rejected
by
women, not to mention P.U.A.s, tradcons, groypers, lobsters, and looksmaxxers—the rainbow flag of virtual misogyny.
When the meeting ends, only Miller and Target remain in the chat. And then something odd happens: Target turns on his computer’s camera. The exchange that ensues is funny, pervy, and startling—and suddenly the play begins to glide along a fresh, unusual path, one that tracks the bond between these two people, who have very different but equally complex relationships with femininity. In the second act, the two rooms merge, so that Miller and Target can inhabit the same space. It’s a date, kind of, or maybe just a hangout, but either way it’s an interaction with a galvanic, destabilizing kick—an attempt to build a bridge between two people who are barely able to make eye contact. At one point, a character screams in terror, “You weren’t streaming, were you?” It’s a reasonable fear: if these two share anything, it’s the knowledge that an invisible digital audience is always watching, thirsty for some catastrophic screwup.
Which brings us to the other audience—the one watching the show. There are theatregoers who might feel resistant to seeing a play so saturated with ugly ideas, let alone one that’s a little sympathetic to the men who hold them. It’s not difficult to imagine a version of “Degenerates” that takes a more palatable, but less interesting, approach to this material, providing a hand-wringing primer on the toxicity of online misogyny—something more like the television show “Adolescence,” which, however elegantly filmed, felt engineered to work as an after-school special for worried parents. In pop culture, incels tend to be portrayed in one of two ways: as a cautionary tale or as a joke. They’re a subject for edutainment, not artistic exploration.
Went—an alum of the Public Theatre’s emerging-playwrights program whose work includes “An Oxford Man,” about the first trans man to get a phalloplasty, and “Initiative,” about Dungeons & Dragons gamers—has significantly stranger fish to fry. A mischievous visionary inspired by slicing verbal stylists such as Oscar Wilde and Noël Coward, Went creates work that dwells on the mutability of human character, depicting sexuality as a liberating wormhole into new identities. In “Degenerates,” she finds provocative parallels between two sets of online isolates who seemed like they should be natural enemies: woman-hating incels and the cadre of mentally fragile, gender-dysphoric teens who came of age in the pandemic. Both groups, she suggests, share a few qualities—a conviction that their bodies are unacceptable, a craving for transformation, a susceptibility to exploitation, and a fascination with cracking the code of gender performance. Perhaps because Went herself is trans, she is refreshingly unconstrained by rules of positive representation, enabling her to create messy, dynamic characters such as Target—a frail figure, played sensitively by Christopher Dylan White, who spends most of the first act curled up like a snail inside a manga-print hoodie, cocooned by stuffies. A screened-out digital native, Target can be icy, brittle, and narcissistic, not to mention alarmingly skilled at manipulation. Yet he’s also capable of real insight and vulnerability. Like any teen-ager, he’s a work in progress, struggling to construct an authentic self inside a universe of deepfakes.
Much of “Degenerates” pops because of its propulsive repartee, which replicates the twisted energy of a chat room at 3
a.m.
: “These feminazis are on Bluesky like ‘if you can’t get a girl, you’re the problem’—like no, bitch, supply is dwindling and I’m the starving class!” But the show is most challenging when the characters get physical, in primal encounters that bear a resemblance to both clowning and pornography. There’s an incendiary wildness to such moments—a willingness to make the audience uncomfortable, to force us into shock, disgust, or arousal—that puts “Degenerates” in conversation with recent plays about female-adolescent rage (“John Proctor Is the Villain,” “Camping,” “Dad Don’t Read This,” “Indian Princesses”) in which no single character is reduced to a mouthpiece for right-think, allowing grottiness and chaos to reign.
I don’t want to spoil the third and final act of “Degenerates,” but I found it satisfying, cathartic, funny, and—as Miller might put it—a bit “hope-pilled.” Went’s canniest gift is her ability to pick the lock of even the cruellest psychic trap, imagining liberation in a way that doesn’t require purity or absolute decency. In a note that opens the script, she writes, “Not all love is selfless; not all mercy is earned.” It’s a Wildean aphorism with a touch of the Biblical, the perfect length for a meme. ♦
